justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish drift from what I would have assessed as the prevailing level of the S&P 500 ETF (SPY) near the time of the forecast, around the low-to-mid 520s. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the last observed price, applying minimal drift since overnight and intraday moves are largely noise around the prior close. For the one-week estimate, I added a small positive drift consistent with the long-run average weekly return of equities, while acknowledging that near-term momentum and macro sentiment were roughly neutral. For the one-month estimate, I extended that same modest drift assumption further, arriving at a figure only slightly above the one-week estimate, reflecting the historically positive but modest expected return over a calendar month in a non-recessionary environment.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily to historical realized volatility of SPY. At the one-day horizon, SPY typically moves within a range of roughly plus or minus 1–1.5%, so a 90% interval spanning about 21 points felt appropriate. At one week, daily volatility compounds and the distribution widens, so I expanded the interval to roughly 38 points. At one month, the interval widens further to about 76 points, reflecting that a month contains enough trading days for volatility to accumulate substantially. I also considered that implied volatility from options markets tends to embed a modest premium above realized vol, which slightly widened my intervals relative to a pure historical-vol approach.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include a surprise shift in Federal Reserve policy communication, such as a more hawkish tone than markets expect at a scheduled meeting or a hot inflation print that reprices rate cut expectations sharply. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in credit markets, a geopolitical shock, or weaker-than-expected earnings from major index constituents could drive SPY well below the lower bound of even the one-month interval. On the upside, a definitive ceasefire in an ongoing geopolitical conflict, a surprisingly dovish Fed pivot, or a blowout jobs or earnings report could push the index above the upper bound.

Finally, it is worth noting that my intervals assume roughly normal return distributions, which underweight fat-tail events. Equity returns historically exhibit negative skew and excess kurtosis, meaning the true probability of an extreme downside move is somewhat higher than a Gaussian model implies. If a systemic risk event materialized — a financial institution stress episode, a sovereign debt scare, or a rapid unwinding of crowded positioning — the realized outcome could fall well outside the bounds I specified, particularly at the one-month horizon where there is simply more time for such events to develop and propagate.
